articles.title: PowerWash Simulator Meets Unpacking In a Cozy Gaming Steam Sleeper Hit
articles.subtitle: Hi there, emotional support Pokia phone! Growing up, the Nancy Drew PC games were my cozy go-tos. They had gorgeous art, well-written stories, and, of course, minigames.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Hi there, emotional support Pokia phone!

Growing up, the Nancy Drew PC games were my cozy go-tos. They had gorgeous art, well-written stories, and, of course, minigames. The series was about solving crimes, but the real draw was the break you’d take to cook pancakes or organize bento boxes. ReStory: Chill Electronics Repairs, from developer Mandragora and publisher tinyBuild, hits a similar formula.

It comes with a healthy dose of nostalgia and the ASMR vibes of games like Unpacking or PowerWash Simulator. Oh, and it’s set in early-aughts Tokyo with an anime-inspired aesthetic and gently-thrumming lofi music.

Clearly a labor of love by the same detail-noticing devs who made I Am Future, ReStory: Chill Electronics Repairs is a narrative shop sim. In it, you play a repair tech. You disassemble, clean, and reassemble everything from officially-licensed Atari consoles (thanks to tinyBuild’s partnership with Atari ) to phones, cameras, and music players. You’re thrown directly into work upon beginning your game.

There’s a to-do list that checks itself off as you set up your workstation and figure out how to open the store. A circular target glows whenever you pick up an item that has a specific place to get to. It’s a little hand-holdy, but the good kind: enough guidance so you’re never lost, and enough left unexplained so you still need to think.

Soon, you’re pulling apart and cleaning your first device: not a Nokia, but a Pokia phone. You start by popping off the back casing, removing highlighted screws, which the game very thoughtfully scoops up for you, and setting aside any components you can’t yet fix in a lower-screen parts box for later — maybe it’ll help with another repair later.

If you’re missing a part entirely, you can hop on the CRT computer and order it online. (The game’s helpful mail carrier will get it to you in seconds. ) Clean, sort, replace, repeat! This same loop remains the same whether you’re cleaning a Pokia phone, an Atari controller, or a PSP — sorry, PMP handheld.

Small clunks as you drop cords and clicks as you fit screen overlays back together offer a nice little touch of immersion and that satisfying ASMR feel. The parts of the experience less dedicated to realism – a progress bar that moves along as you clean a component, the animated dust clouds whooshing off your brush – transform a chore into a true delight.

Caring for your various gadgets is completed via pointing, clicking, and dragging…which is, admittedly, a lot of continuous dragging. You’ll be holding down the left mouse button a lot. And there are situations where you cannot finish a repair with the parts on your desk, which can feel confusing. The game responds to this slight roadblock by prompting you to re-box the pieces for later. The right pieces will come to you; all you need to do is keep watching and waiting.

Playing this game for a few hours felt truly meditative. It also felt like opening the door to my childhood home. Oh hello weathered Atari poster on the wall! Hi again, gray ‘90s CRT computer that I definitely had growing up! Good to see you, cassette tape with the ribbon all wound out!

But, don’t worry, there’s a story tying it all together, too. What’s that about something baffling happening to the previous repair master at your tiny establishment? Eh, that’s probably important. But right now, there is only you… and the cozily dim lighting… and the Tamagotchi analog you’re fixing for the child who asked for your help. Will you charge them, or is work for kids pro bono? You decide.

Early on, you’ll meet characters who dispense tantalizing narrative details. Secondhand marketplace sellers will allegedly mislead you about a device’s condition when you’re sourcing parts? Scandal! Your landlord shows up demanding rent, but then coaches you to charge more for a repair? Maybe he’s nice! A bucket descends from above, introducing your upstairs neighbor who needs help repairing their joystick so they can compete in a Pac-Man championship? I for sure want to help them, sign me up!

Heads up if you play: You will lose track of time. But that’s endearingly echoed in the game itself. When you set up your workspace, you can place an alarm clock on your desk. I settled into a rhythm of checking the time before a repair, completing my tasks, shipping the fixed piece, and checking the clock again – always bemused by how much in-game time had passed. My player character and I are both engrossed in what we’re doing, and letting hours drift by.

But it’s time well spent. Maybe in the next few hours, I’ll learn what’s up with the strange phone number I found in the first Pokia I repaired. Only time will tell. And in the meantime, I’ve got a broken Motorola – ah, I mean Autorolla “Razor” to tend to.

ReStory: Chill Electronics Repairs is out now on Steam. The game was reviewed on PC using a prerelease download code provided by tinyBuild. You can find additional information about Polygon’s ethics policy here.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: The MacStories Public Beta Preview
articles.subtitle: The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.

It’s not my final take on Golden Gate by any means; after all, I’ve only been using it for about a month, and there will be several more turns in the beta cycle between now and the public release. However, I’ve used Golden Gate long enough to help you make an informed decision about whether or not to install the public beta now.

Of course, it’s impossible for me to account for everyone’s unique Mac setups when considering Golden Gate’s stability, but it’s worth reiterating what I’ve said in past previews: modern Apple betas have been consistently stable. That’s to say, the risks of using the public beta are modest. It’s been years since I’ve had a critical app fail or lost data.

I never go into beta season without a backup plan, though. If something goes terribly wrong, I have backups, backups of those backups, and alternate Macs I can switch to in the event of a disaster. I don’t expect to have to go to Plan B, but if you’re going to jump on the Beta Bus, you should have a Plan B, too.

Okay, you’ve been warned. Let’s get to the fun part.

Supported By

Inoreader

Every year’s macOS update is a little different, but Golden Gate is more different than most. Instead of focusing on tentpole features and apps (with the exception of a new Siri app), macOS 27’s updates fall into three broad categories:

refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language,

hundreds of system-level changes intended to improve your Mac’s performance, and

Apple Intelligence, which includes the new Siri app as well as many other AI additions to existing system apps.

It’s been a while since the “Snow Leopard Moment.”

With so many past macOS updates focusing on system apps, it’s refreshing to see Apple take a more holistic system-level approach, which harkens back to how most people remember OS X Snow Leopard. In fact, during WWDC briefings, Apple representatives likened the Golden Gate update to Snow Leopard before anyone in the room even asked about it.

Snow Leopard is remembered as a release that focused on performance over features. The reality is that the update also introduced its fair share of new features, but many were less splashy from a user-facing standpoint. They were under-the-hood updates that made the Mac work better without users having to think about it much. In that sense, Golden Gate has a lot in common with Snow Leopard.

Other than the brand new Siri app, you probably won’t notice that much is different when you first launch the new version. But over time, the changes will reveal themselves, adding up to a whole that – with few exceptions – is greater than the parts.

So let’s take a closer look at how Liquid Glass has evolved, the most significant system changes, and what it’s like to use Siri and other Apple Intelligence updates in Golden Gate’s public beta.

Design

Windows stand out from each other more, and the sidebar runs edge to edge in Golden Gate.

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.subtitle: (Left to right): Annotate, Kickabout, and Undolly. For the most part, I’m going to focus on Mac apps with these columns, because that’s where the action seems to be these days.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
For the most part, I’m going to focus on Mac apps with these columns, because that’s where the action seems to be these days. But iOS remains a vibrant platform, too, and every now and again, we’ll look at some of the interesting apps being created for iPhones and iPads. This is one of those now and agains.

Want to see your app included in a future round-up? Get in touch at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of your app, and you just might make the cut.

Kickabout

The World Cup is just a memory now, but if you’re missing the daily infusion of soccer (or football, depending on what part of the globe you’re reading this from), Kickabout brings the action back to your iOS device in a very condensed form.

Kickabout will be immediately familiar to anyone who’s ever gathered around a foosball table in a rec room, with a look that will bring a smile to the face of Subbuteo tabletop football aficionados. You take charge of an 8-player team, with players only free to move about certain areas of the pitch. (No length-of-the-field Maradona-esque wonder golazos for your squad.

) You use your finger to drag your players around, swiping any which way to boot the ball toward the goal as you look to rack up the most goals in each 2-minute match.

Goals and shots off the post earn you points, which translates to tickets that you cash in to collect various national teams, from the U.S. all the way to newly minted world champion Spain. You can also buy gear, including stands for your virtual stadium. It’s a fun element that adds to Kickabout’s replayability as you try to assemble your own World Cup field.

Kickabout has both single-player and dual-player modes, though I found the latter to be a little cramped for my iPhone 17 screen. I imagine head-to-head matches are much more enjoyable on the iPad. Still, Kickabout offers plenty of fun even for single players, as you try to master the game’s different difficulty levels.

Kickabout is free to download, and a $3 in-app purchase gets rid of any ads.

Undolly

The Photos app has a built-in tool to weed out duplicate images, but if you find yourself taking a lot of photos, Undolly brings a whole suite of tools that promise to bring order to your iOS device’s photo library. Besides getting rid of duplicates, the mobile app also lists large videos taking up space in your library, rounds up any screenshots you may have stashed somewhere and keeps tabs on other potential space-takers like RAW, timelapse and animated images.

The value of Undolly will depend heavily on how you use your photo library. For instance, I take a lot of screenshots for articles that I don’t always remember to delete, and the app helped me track down some that were three to five years old. I also appreciate Undolly’s swipable comparisons of similar shots, so you can see for yourself whether the images differ enough to keep.

Undolly’s algorithm also rates images by their framing, quality and expressiveness of subject to better help you determine the shots that deserve a place in your library.

While it’s free to download initially, you will have to subscribe to Undolly to use its features, with a free three-day trial letting you get the lay of the land. After that, a monthly subscription costs $4, while annual and lifetime payments go for $15 and $40, respectively.

VWLSS

Nearly five years after Wordle first appeared, we’re still living in a golden age for daily word puzzles. Add VWLSS and its daily serving of mobile word play to the pile, though there are some unique iPhone elements that could help this free offering earn a place in your regular rotation of gameplay.

You have eight words to guess, each tied to a specific category and with all the vowels stripped out. It’s up to you to figure out the actual word, which you can do either by typing in the answer or using a handy speech feature. I prefer talking to typing, though I’m still sore that my guess of “Bob Barker” in the game show hosts category was misheard as “Bob Parker.” Revenge will be mine tomorrow, I guess.

articles.title: My Hero Academia author’s new horror manga Quit Laughing, Shijima was just released in English
articles.subtitle: Quit Laughing, Shijima just launched on the Shonen Jump app. Related After the My Hero Academia anime 's final season ended late last year, there has been plenty of curiosity about what's next for Kohei Horikoshi, the comic artist behind the manga.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Quit Laughing, Shijima just launched on the Shonen Jump app.

Related

After the My Hero Academia anime 's final season ended late last year, there has been plenty of curiosity about what's next for Kohei Horikoshi, the comic artist behind the manga. Not long ago, he announced a surprising change of pace for his next work. Quit Laughing, Shijima is a horror/romance one-shot that was just released on the Shonen Jump app and website this morning.

The 61-page story centers on Azumi, a second-year high school student with a crush on his upperclassman, Shijima, who is known for her charming personality and boisterous laugh. From there, things don’t exactly go like a typical meet-cute. The standalone story was released in Japan on Aug. 10 in the 37/38 issue of Weekly Shonen Jump, with a simulpub digital release in English on the Shonen Jump App.

It is Horikoshi’s first work in Shonen Jump since the My Hero Academia manga ran from 2014 to 2024. Before that, the author wrote Barrage and Oumagadoki Zoo for the magazine. My Hero Academia has quickly become one of the best-selling manga of all time, having surpassed 100 million sales, putting it in rare company alongside other recent hits like Jujutsu Kaisen, Demon Slayer, and Attack on Titan.

The anime finished its official run in December, 2025 with an explosive eighth season from Bones Film that delivered excellent animation and cathartic character moments. On May 2, 2026, Bones released the “More” bonus special, which acted as a similarly satisfying epilogue. Lastly, there was the six-minute “ I Am A Hero Too ” mini-episode that adapted the manga’s final bonus material.

In the years since My Hero Academia ’s manga ended in 2024, fans have joked that “ unemployed Horikoshi ” is one of the most visually impressive comic artists of the moment — he released detailed illustrations to coincide with new episodes of the show. With Horikoshi having finally put out his highly anticipated new one-shot that's in a completely different genre, it will be interesting to see what the author does for his next serialized work.

You can read Quit Laughing, Shijima for free here.

Kohei Horikoshi is working on a horror romance manga that will be out in early August.

articles.title: Always choose the good soap
articles.subtitle: (Angelo D’Amico/Shutterstock) I’ve been thinking about soap again. Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation: We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’ve been thinking about soap again.

Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation:

We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we usually do. Because I’m me, I started thinking about Apple. Like Apple, the nice hotel’s brand promise is that it’s a nice hotel.

If the hotel didn’t clean its rooms well, didn’t provide soap that smelled nice, didn’t maintain the in-room refrigerator, didn’t clean the swimming pool, it would probably decrease its expenses and increase its profit margin. But over time, it would lose its niceness and become a lousy, overpriced hotel.

Earlier this month, John Gruber wrote about how he hopes incoming Apple CEO John Ternus can perform a bit of a reset on Apple’s advertising strategy. In recent months Apple has announced that it’s adding ads to Apple Maps, and ( as John has documented ) it’s allowed incredibly low-quality, scammy ads to infest Apple News.

While Apple can spin adding ads to Apple Maps as a revolutionary new way for businesses to be discovered, it’s telling that its initial announcement was hidden inside a press release about an entirely different product, and introduced as “Enhanced Discoverability in Apple Maps.

” Those choices show that this isn’t something Apple is actually proud of—and that the people in charge of communicating and explaining Apple’s decisions to the world are at odds with those who are making the decisions about expanding revenue.

Apple also recently expanded App Store ads, creating more clutter at the top of App Store search results. It similarly pitched this as an opportunity for developers—but of course, it’s really an opportunity for developers to take a portion of the money they make from the App Store after Apple’s cut and hand it right back to Apple so that their apps don’t become invisible. What a racket.

But Apple’s approach to grinding out additional revenue doesn’t stop with advertising. The recent release of Apple Creator Studio should’ve been a highlight, because it groups a bunch of useful creative apps in one place for a reasonable price. Instead, its launch was marred by the inclusion of Apple’s free productivity apps in the bundle, requiring users to download new versions and (at least initially) display aggressive subscription promotions in the Numbers, Pages, and Keynote interface.

To this day, you’re confronted with an ad for Creator Studio every time you create a new document in those apps, and their default toolbars contain buttons that won’t work unless you subscribe to the bundle.

As a result, Apple has essentially turned its free productivity suite—software that was designed to enhance the inherent value of Apple’s products—into a freemium package with upsell to a creative professional subscription bundle that’s irrelevant (and a terrible value! ) for most of its existing users.

There are many more examples. Using notifications to promote subscriptions and badging the Settings app to push AppleCare plans are among the ways Apple has chosen to intervene in the user experience to drive revenue.

I’m actually not opposed to the idea that Apple should communicate opportunities for its customers to get more out of their devices—but it should be careful not to cross the line into actively annoying those customers. If someone doesn’t want to see what you offer, you need to accept that and go away—not keep needling them. Apple often falls on the wrong side of that line.

Which brings me back to the hotel soap.

Apple’s most valuable asset is its brand. Not its real estate, not its intellectual property, not even any particular product. Even the mighty iPhone has no value if, over time, the traits that differentiate it from competitor products are erased. Apple’s brand has always stood for higher quality products—you pay more, but you get more. Apple has never wanted to be the low-price leader.

It didn’t put stickers on the first Intel Macs to get some marketing dollars from Intel. It doesn’t load up new Macs with loads of lousy bundled third-party software like so many PCs do.

Those are choices Apple has made that cost the company revenue, but they’ve got a bigger purpose. They reinforce the brand.

Opting not to add more revenue to the bottom line is a difficult choice for anyone working at a profit-driven corporation. I used to be in that position at my former employer, defending the overall product against a constant stream of advertising and biz-dev deal proposals that would add incremental revenue. Believe me, arguing to corporate executives that we should leave money on the table is a deeply uncomfortable role to take on—but it’s vital if you care about the bigger picture.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

articles.title: Beast of Reincarnation Has a Difficulty Problem
articles.subtitle: Taking it (too) easy Related In the distant future, the world is in tough shape. Emma, a hero with the skill and fortitude to save the world, wanders a harsh wasteland that is hellbent on eliminating humanity.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Taking it (too) easy

Related

In the distant future, the world is in tough shape. Emma, a hero with the skill and fortitude to save the world, wanders a harsh wasteland that is hellbent on eliminating humanity. Beast of Reincarnation, the new action RPG from Game Freak, chronicles her journey and puts players in charge of seeing it through to its conclusion.

The game is tough, and at times its mechanics can feel nigh-inscrutable. Brief opening tutorials walk players through convoluted systems as they deal with the reality that a single blow might mark the end of their progress. At least, that’s how it all works in Normal mode. But there is a “Story” (read: easy) setting that is considerably more forgiving. Thing is, Beast of Reincarnation ’s easy mode is not a great fit.

As noted, enemies in Normal mode pose a genuine threat. Emma sneaks through fields of flowers with her dog Koo running by her side. He’s a faithful companion, even if he sucks the fun out of discovering hidden treasure on the battlefield. He’ll typically point out an enemy that is waiting to stab her in the back, but if he doesn’t? Well, that could be the end of her.

Even when Emma has a full life meter, a vicious golem could potentially assassinate her with a single well-placed thrust, before she even knows he’s there. Head-on battles with some of the more elite enemies scattered across the map can also prove perilous. Boss battles with the large and fearsome Nushi monsters Emma hunts might end in mere seconds.

That’s fine, though. I’m not complaining. By default, the game relies on a stiff challenge to make the adventure feel worthwhile, and it handsomely rewards players who persevere. Simply accept that it’s that kind of game and you’ll do fine. Don’t accept it and, well, there’s always Story mode.

Whatever setting you choose, Beast of Reincarnation expects you to make the most of its systems. You’re supposed to run into trouble, then figure out how to resolve it by equipping better armor, upgraded weapons, and spirit stones. You’re supposed to master unique skills, unlocked from a skill tree, which let Emma deal crushing blows, recover health while standing amidst impromptu flower gardens, and inject stimpacks while engaged in close encounters of the boss kind.

The difference between Story mode and Normal mode is jarring, however. A lethal monster that once felled even an over-leveled Emma with one quick strike suddenly shaves off only a tiny sliver of health with each blow landed. It develops a glass jaw, falling quickly to a barrage of arrows it shrugged aside on the higher settings. And it moves without the same sense of purpose.

I’ll admit it: when I first played Beast of Reincarnation, I was absolutely terrible at it. I scrapped with the first Nushi several times and almost beat it, but I always fell just short because I hadn’t bothered mastering Emma’s most lethal moves. I kept trying to snipe my adversary from a distance, and it responded by eliminating the space between us in two seconds flat while I fumbled to change between my projectile weapons.

Finally, because the game lets players shift difficulty levels whenever it suits them, I tried my luck in Story mode. That experience briefly left me wondering if it was even possible for Emma to fail.

I’ve never minded when games give me the option of taking it easy. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild presented me with a manageable wilderness that I was happy to enjoy on its terms until I finally decided to look for ways to make Hyrule more dangerous. I’ve had a good time with all sorts of difficulty settings, which is why I feel that Beast of Reincarnation ’s developers missed an opportunity.

The game’s difficulty options suggest they were meant to provide a proper range of experiences. They just didn’t go far enough.

The Story setting really is, as it notes in its menus, for “those who wish to focus on the story.” Beast of Reincarnation makes the adventure more manageable for genre newcomers and casual players or folks who can’t grasp the myriad systems it introduces and doesn’t properly explain (except in tedious tutorial screens players will be tempted to ignore).

The accommodation certainly makes sense. I’m not always prepared to tend gardens in the apocalypse so that my friend can make me delicious meals that improve my stats, no matter how often the characters suggest that I really ought to. And I’m not often eager to explore the branches of multiple skill trees, piecing together brilliant skills that will let me thrive.

( Beast of Reincarnation ’s skill trees are particularly byzantine. ) After a rough day’s work, I might just want to hack my way to victory without spending too much time thinking about parrying windows.

Story mode in Beast of Reincarnation is generous with its damage reduction. But when it’s the only option this side of an excessively demanding experience, it risks turning too many elements of the adventure into filler. Prizes for exploration and the constant challenge of continued survival lose their meaning.

And the nodes on the skill tree hardly appeal, because I don’t even need to rely on the skills they impart to stand a chance against the next boss. The Story mode, in other words, turns down the difficulty a bit too much from Normal.

articles.title: How to keep your Mac awake, even when your MacBook lid is closed
articles.subtitle: macOS is designed to put your Mac to sleep when it is not being used. That is usually exactly what you want. Sleep saves power, protects battery life, and keeps a MacBook from running when it is closed and stuffed in a bag.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
macOS is designed to put your Mac to sleep when it is not being used. That is usually exactly what you want. Sleep saves power, protects battery life, and keeps a MacBook from running when it is closed and stuffed in a bag.

Sometimes tasks like downloads, backups, remote sessions, and AI coding need a temporary exception. Fortunately, there are some great Mac apps for giving you this control.

Limited solutions that are included with macOS

Apple gives you some control in System Settings.

On macOS, you can go to System Settings > Lock Screen to change when the display turns off, and on Mac laptops you can use System Settings > Battery > Options to prevent automatic sleeping on the power adapter when the display is off.

Apple also supports using a Mac laptop with the lid closed when it is connected to power and paired with an external display, keyboard, and mouse or trackpad.

I generally prefer not to make those settings permanent. Most of the time, I want my Mac to sleep normally. What I want instead is a quick, intentional override that I can turn on for a specific job and turn off when I am done.

For that, there are three Mac utilities worth knowing.

KeepingYouAwake is the simple one-click toggle

KeepingYouAwake is the utility that has lived in my Mac menu bar the longest.

It is free, lightweight, and built around the same basic idea that made Caffeine popular years ago: click a menu bar icon, and your Mac stays awake. Click it again, and your Mac returns to its normal sleep behavior.

I started using KeepingYouAwake years ago when Macs moved to Retina displays. Caffeine, the classic coffee-cup utility, did not make that transition to high-resolution design.

KeepingYouAwake became the simple replacement. It honors the spirit of Caffeine with no dashboard or complex automation. It’s just a reliable on/off switch for the Mac’s default sleep behavior.

You can activate it indefinitely or for preset durations, and it can automatically disable itself when your MacBook battery drops below a set level. It supports Retina displays and Dark Mode, and under the hood it uses Apple’s built-in caffeinate command-line utility.

The important limitation: KeepingYouAwake is not the closed-lid solution. Its own documentation is clear that, because of macOS limitations and thermal considerations, it only prevents sleep on desktop Macs and portable Macs with the lid open.

That makes KeepingYouAwake ideal for the simple stuff: reading, presentations, screen recordings, long downloads, or any time you are still using the Mac and just do not want the screen or system to nod off. It is the utility I use as my everyday “do not sleep yet” toggle.

Amphetamine is the gold standard for closed-lid sessions

When I actually want to close my MacBook and keep a task running, Amphetamine is the app I open.
